1.hint: 先听清新闻开头指控的内容，并区分喂鸟与虐待动物。
1.explanation: D。开头的“charged with ... violating ... city law”明确是违反城市法规的指控，不是虐待动物。邻居抱怨和喂鸟只是报道背景，不能替代指控内容。
1.prompt: What do we learn from the report about the 55-year-old woman?

2.hint: 关注新闻结尾局长对问题何时能得到控制的判断。
2.explanation: A。局长说“it will take months to get the problem under control”，说明解决鼠患需要时间。其余选项转移到保护动物、免责或处罚原则，新闻结尾没有这些结论。
2.prompt: What did the director of the city administration say at the end of the news report?

3.hint: 听清NASA招募志愿者后要求他们实际从事的活动。
3.explanation: B。原文明确说志愿者“work in an environment similar to Mars”，选项resembling Mars与similar to Mars同义；并不是在真实火星上工作或与宇航员通信。
3.prompt: What does NASA require the paid volunteers to do?

4.hint: 注意报道对食品来源和供应方式的具体说明。
4.explanation: A。“Food will all be ready-to-eat space food”对应现成的即食食物。虽然可能种植物，原文特别排除电影中的土豆，不能把部分种植推断为全部自产。
4.prompt: What will the participants in the project eat?

5.hint: 关注市长的具体动作，而不是获奖运动员的动作。
5.explanation: C。报道开头说市长为“biting the Olympic gold medal of a softball player”道歉，之后叙述他戴上金牌并咬了一口。关键动作是咬金牌，不是颁奖或划伤。
5.prompt: What does the news report say about the Japanese mayor Takashi Kawamura?

6.hint: 留意offered后面表达市长愿意承担的责任。
6.explanation: D。市长说金牌没有损坏，但“offered to pay for the cost of a new one”。因此他提出支付新金牌费用；原文没有提议修理、再拍照或向奥委会道歉。
6.prompt: What did mayor Takashi Kawamura offer to do?

7.hint: 听清一些奥运选手怎样形容自己对奖牌的态度。
7.explanation: C。“they treat their medals as treasures”直接对应选项。后面的轻拿轻放是在说明珍视程度，不能据此推断他们绝不让别人触碰或一定锁在安全处。
7.prompt: What did some Olympians say they would do with their medals?

8.hint: 注意女方对电脑屏幕上橙色物体的解释。
8.explanation: A。女方说买了能阻挡蓝光的plastic sheet，并且手机上也用这种覆盖物，因此电脑屏幕被塑料片覆盖。其他选项的软件、装饰贴纸或手机连接没有出现。
8.prompt: What did the woman do to her computer?

9.hint: 留意女方用but补充蓝光来源的部分。
9.explanation: B。她说蓝光包括自然光，“but it also includes light that isn't natural”，随后列举电子设备。不能把蓝光一概等同于伤害或认为它能帮助入睡。
9.prompt: What does the woman say about blue light?

10.hint: 区分男方自己描述的原因与女方给出的健康解释。
10.explanation: D。男方承认几个月睡眠不足“because I have too much work to do”。他当时自认为状态良好，因此本题问他的原因应选工作过多，不是游戏或已患疾病。
10.prompt: Why does the man say he hasn't slept enough for months?

11.hint: 听清研究结果如何修正人们原先对睡眠重要性的认识。
11.explanation: B。女方说“sleep is probably even more important than we thought”，对应睡眠比原先认为的更重要。肥胖和心脏病是睡眠不足的潜在后果，并非蓝光单独被认定为首要原因。
11.prompt: What has the woman learned from the research she has read?

12.hint: 注意双方都表示厌烦的那个童年问题。
12.explanation: A。男方讨厌成人问“What I wanted to be when I grew up”，女方立即表示同感。问题是长大后的职业，而不是喜爱的卡通、游戏或课后活动。
12.prompt: What question were both speakers fed up with when they were kids?

13.hint: 留意女儿三个回答中成年人特别喜欢的最后一个。
13.explanation: C。女儿说篮球运动员、流行歌手和机械工程师；女方随后说“Adults love that last one”，last one指机械工程师，被认为兼有务实与雄心。
13.prompt: What occupation do adults see as both sensible and ambitious according to the woman?

14.hint: 将女方赞赏的目标与她强调的想象力联系起来。
14.explanation: C。她喜欢女儿想当“Queen of the Clouds”，并解释这种目标来自“boundless imaginations”。因此欣赏富于想象的目标设定，不是只强调现实或实用。
14.prompt: What kind of goal-setting does the woman like to see in children?

15.hint: 关注对话末尾对父母帮助孩子方式的总结。
15.explanation: B。女方说应“helping our kids understand who they are”，即帮助孩子认识自己，即使要放下父母预设的身份。不是要求孩子实现父母指定的职业梦想。
15.prompt: What does the woman suggest adults should do?

16.hint: 注意文章介绍进入非洲市场的手机具有什么基本能力。
16.explanation: D。电话公司正引入“Internet-ready phones”，且出售价格低至20美元的智能机，因此是在推广能联网的手机。价格是扩大可及性的手段，不是全面铺设网络的声明。
16.prompt: What are a number of phone companies trying to do in Africa?

17.hint: 对比多数公司的追求与KaiOS相反的设计方向。
17.explanation: A。多数公司追求更强性能，KaiOS却保留基本能力、削减成本并延长电池寿命。其设计针对负担能力和供电不足，因此满足非洲用户的实际需求。
17.prompt: How do KaiOS smartphones differ from smartphones of most other companies?

18.hint: 听清instead of所连接的两种手机操作方式。
18.explanation: B。原文说“Instead of a touchscreen, they're controlled with an old-school keypad”。因此配备传统按键；触屏恰好是被替代的方式，不能混淆。
18.prompt: What are KaiOS smartphones equipped with?

19.hint: 留意for years引出的过去情况，不要与当前价格相混淆。
19.explanation: C。开头说过去回收塑料制品“was cheap”，而化石燃料塑料更贵，既环保也经济。后文现在回收塑料贵72美元是在描述变化，不能代替过去情况。
19.prompt: What is said about using recycled plastic to make plastic products in the past?

20.hint: 注意解释新塑料价格下降时出现的because。
20.explanation: D。原文把新塑料更便宜归因于美国“a boom in petroleum chemical production”，即石油化工生产繁荣。没有说回收设施进步或大规模制造能力才是本题原因。
20.prompt: What has led to more competitive prices for new plastic?

21.hint: 把征税门槛与扩大回收塑料供应的措施合起来判断。
21.explanation: D。英国计划向回收材料占比不足30%的企业征税，还拟增加回收塑料供给。两类措施共同鼓励企业更多使用回收塑料，不能只看成提高新塑料产量。
21.prompt: What does the UK government plan to do about plastic?

22.hint: 注意Dreamery所出售的服务及其收费方式。
22.explanation: B。Dreamery以25美元出售安静暗室中45分钟的小憩，“This is a nap joint”，不是旅馆。收费休息服务是报道对这家企业的核心介绍。
22.prompt: What do we learn about the Dreamery, a business in Manhattan?

23.hint: 结合讲话者随后对下午工作状态的描述理解这个反问。
23.explanation: C。讲话者反问午睡是否值25美元并给肯定答案，又让人观察下午2:30的状态，以说明午睡的重要性。不是要求去搜集研究或宣传某家店的优惠。
23.prompt: Why does the speaker ask us to look at the world around us at 2:30 in the afternoon?

24.hint: 留意工作质量和数量直接取决于哪一种能力。
24.explanation: B。讲话者说工作的质量和数量“emerges directly from my ability to concentrate”，因此二者直接受专注能力影响。工作地点和工时只是背景，不是他指出的直接决定因素。
24.prompt: What do we learn about the quantity and quality of the speaker's work?

25.hint: 关注最后一段讲话者认为奇怪的办公室观念。
25.explanation: A。他的朋友说老板把午睡视为懒惰，讲话者对此觉得奇怪，随后说明合适午睡能加倍一天的专注力。奇怪的是这种负面看法，而不是午睡收费本身。
25.prompt: What does the speaker say he finds odd?

26.hint: 先判断and连接的两个动作需要相同形式。
26.explanation: L，sew，缝制。create fabric and sew it into a shirt shape是两个并列动作，空格需动词原形；布料制成衣服靠缝制，mend指修补已有破损，不符合生产过程。

27.hint: 观察the most后与clothing material的修饰关系。
27.explanation: B，abundant，丰富的。the most后、名词短语clothing material前需要形容词，文章说明棉是大量使用的服装材料。abundant描述供应丰富，intense描述强度，不合语义。

28.hint: 把这个插入语与前面给出的精确用水量联系起来。
28.explanation: E，exact，准确的。to be exact是固定插入表达“准确地说”，用来限定每件衬衫2700升的具体数字；空格在be后需要形容词，不是要求或索取的动词意义。

29.hint: 注意mind-blowing修饰的名词以及前后提到的数字。
29.explanation: N，statistics，统计数据。视频展示棉服生产令人震惊的数字，前文2700升也是例子。mind-blowing需要名词作中心语，statistics与数据主题对应，不是abstracts摘要。

30.hint: 判断is与becoming之间的词应如何修饰变化趋势。
30.explanation: F，increasingly，越来越。is becoming是谓语，空格需副词；全文强调净水日益成为热门资源，所以increasingly表达变化程度。nearly只表示差不多，没有持续增长的意思。

31.hint: 根据and cotton industries判断它所指的相关产业。
31.explanation: O，textile，纺织业。空格与cotton共同修饰industries，文章讨论布料和衣服生产用水，因此是纺织和棉花产业。conscience良心与生产行业语境无关。

32.hint: 关注spread后面要传播的环境信息或认识。
32.explanation: C，awareness，意识。spread awareness of how environmentally harmful cotton is表示提高人们对棉花环境影响的认识。此处需要名词；conscience表示道德良心，不是对具体风险的认识。

33.hint: 注意百分数前的副词表示近似程度。
33.explanation: I，nearly，接近。cut down by nearly 40 percent表示用水量可减少接近40%。空格修饰百分数，应填近似程度副词；increasingly通常修饰动态趋势，不直接表达约百分之四十。

34.hint: 判断from后面表示节水原因的动作形式。
34.explanation: K，reducing，减少。from后接动名词，reducing the demands of cotton production表示减少棉花生产需求从而节水。reckoning虽然也是-ing形式，但表示估计或认为，不能说明节水原因。

35.hint: 注意as从句需要与water supplies搭配的谓语。
35.explanation: M，shrink，缩减。as water supplies shrink表示随着供水减少，农民和消费者更应注意环境影响。空格须有时态谓语，reducing不能单独作此从句的谓语。

36.hint: 寻找描述气象语音服务成本和操作难度的词组。
36.explanation: F段说“The service was designed to be cheap and easy to run”，与题干inexpensive and easy to use同义。主体是Francis Dittoh的气象服务，而不是一般语音助手的市场价格。

37.hint: 关注语音填写病人表格如何改变医生的时间分配。
37.explanation: K段说明医生口述速度为打字三倍，因此“less time on administration and more time with patients”。题干take care of patients归纳这一结果，L段虽也讲诊所系统但没有这句时间对比。

38.hint: 寻找把语音转成文字的困难及其原因同时出现的段落。
38.explanation: H段指出语音识别是最难解决的问题之一，因为“as many ways to pronounce things as ... people”。题干同时概括了转换难度和发音差异，不能只凭某段也提到AI就匹配。

39.hint: 注意题干里的不能阅读与信息被拒于门外两个要点。
39.explanation: D段说不识字的非洲农民“denied crucial information the web offers many others”。unable to read对应illiterate，don't have access对应denied，两个信息点都符合。

40.hint: 定位针对用户直接投放广告的担忧，不要混同一般隐私。
40.explanation: J段末尾说人们担心助手被用来“deliver advertising directly to us”，对应send ads directly。该段同时谈隐私，但本题具体问的是广告利用。

41.hint: 找使用者双手正忙着做其他事情时的便利。
41.explanation: M段开头说“Using voice also makes sense when you're doing other things with your hands”，再举做饭和开车例子。hands are occupied就是双手在忙，与语音输入适用场景一致。

42.hint: 注意将语音作为网络主要交互方式的预测。
42.explanation: C段说语音可能取代typing and clicking，成为“the main way to interact online”。题干mainly on voice正是对此预测的概括，而不是说目前所有交互都已改成语音。

43.hint: 关注建立这种网络的复杂性，而不是它的潜在受益者。
43.explanation: G段明确说“building the spoken web ... isn't straightforward”，之后解释跨领域对话仍很远。by no means an easy task对应isn't straightforward，都是强调建设困难。

44.hint: 寻找天气信息与农民实际播种、灌溉活动的关系。
44.explanation: E段说知道何时下雨对于播种、灌溉或放牧的农民是“vital”。题干extremely important与vital同义，F段介绍气象服务实现方式而不是这项必要性。

45.hint: 注意手机持续收集数据与隐私担忧之间的因果。
45.explanation: J段说手机一直在身边并持续“collecting data about us all the time”，这“raised privacy concerns”。题干个人信息收集与concerned about privacy分别对应这两个信息点。

46.hint: 找首段广告如何把大房子与勤奋工作联系起来。
46.explanation: B。首段“a reward for hard work and diligence”直接对应a reward for industriousness。作者在描述营销说法，不是在主张无家可归者应获得奢侈品或所有幸福都依赖豪宅。

47.hint: 关注公共设施减少后的影响范围，避免绝对化推断。
47.explanation: A。第三段说明公共空间私有化减少大家可用的设施，导致“a reduced quality of life for many”。B、C把局部影响夸大为不再社交或完全无法游泳，D转向未被说明的私人生活。

48.hint: 理解ethical questions所指的问题类型。
48.explanation: A。第四段直接说大住房趋势“poses ethical questions”，随后问富人享受是否依赖低薪劳工和穷人设施减少。因此是道德原则问题，不只是计算劳动成本或推广生活方式。

49.hint: 结合第四段两个问句与第五段的否定理解作者立场。
49.explanation: D。作者不接受富人的设施增加意味着穷人的设施减少的制度；D概括为富人舒适生活以穷人的损失为代价。B只讲价格、C只讲住房，均缩窄或改变了文章讨论的制度问题。

50.hint: 区分作者主张增加公共空间与把所有私产一律共享。
50.explanation: C。末段提出“create more publicly accessible spaces and amenities for all”，即创造更多公共空间供所有人享受。文章没有要求把全部私有空间或全部设施转为公共所有。

51.hint: 从首段对创业群体的总体描述判断比较对象。
51.explanation: B。首句说创业群体具有“higher-than-average ambition”，即比通常水平更有野心。willing to take more risks不是冒生命危险，也不能据此说他们所有积极品质都比常人多。

52.hint: 把this指回前一段的成功概率判断，再看后句转折。
52.explanation: A。前段认为更有动力设目标就更可能成功，接着说并非总如此，并解释极端野心可能弊大于利。否定的是野心与成功概率之间的必然关系，不是否定全部积极品质。

53.hint: 注意作者称vital的能力与过度执着的弊端形成对照。
53.explanation: B。第四段说适应新环境“is vital if you want to be a successful entrepreneur”。执着单一目标会阻碍适应，因此坚持原愿景、拒绝转向都与作者认为重要的能力相反。

54.hint: 看最有野心的创业者怎样解释失败，不要与适度野心者混淆。
54.explanation: C。第五段说对最有野心者，失败被视为“disastrous, and impossible to recover from”，即事业终结。下一段把失败当学习经验说的是野心有限者，不能移用到本题主体。

55.hint: 关注健康、幸福与传统成功的价值比较。
55.explanation: D。第七段说有野心者较可能取得物质成功，但这不保证健康幸福，并反问缺了二者其他还有何意义。由此可知应优先健康幸福，而不是一味模仿极端野心或只讨论创业风险。

listening.transcript: A woman was charged with allegedly violating a Rhode Island city law against feeding wild animals. The 55-year-old woman's neighbors blame her for making the area's rat problem worse. Newly installed cameras captured several rats active in the middle of the day. Neighbors say that it's even worse during the night. The woman and her parents, who own the home, told reporters that she's being charged for feeding birds. "Who would have known just loving animals gets you that much trouble,"she said. It is prohibited to feed any wild animals including birds in Rhode Island City. Nevertheless, while the woman's intention was to feed birds, it is clear that rats were also benefiting. Anthony Moretti, director of the city administration, said he saw more than 20 rats near the woman's home. He said it will take months to get the problem under control.

To prepare for eventually sending astronauts to Mars, NASA began taking applications Friday for four people to live for a year in Mars Dune Alpha. That's a 1,700-square-foot Martian habitat inside a building in Houston. The paid volunteers will work in an environment similar to Mars. They will have limited communications with family, restricted food and resources. NASA is planning three experiments with the first one starting in the fall next year. Food will all be ready-to-eat space food. Some plants will be grown, but not potatoes like in the movie The Martian. "We want to understand how humans perform in them," said lead scientists Grace Douglas."We are looking at Mars realistic situations." The application process open Friday and they're not seeking just anybody. The requirements are strict, including a master's degree in a science, engineering or math field or pilot experience. Only American citizens or permanent U. S. residents are acceptable. Applicants must be between 30 and 55 and in good physical health. Attitude is key, said former Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield. He said the participants need to be super competent, resourceful, and not relying on other people to feel comfortable.

A Japanese mayor apologized Thursday for biting the Olympic gold medal of a softball player. Nagoya mayor Takashi Kawamura had praised athlete, Miu Goto, during a public media event. He asked her to put the medal around his neck. Kawamura then bit into it. Biting a medal in front of journalists and photographers has become a common pose for Olympic medalists. However, it is only for the winners themselves, not others. "I'm really sorry that I hurt the treasure of the gold medalist," Kawamura told reporters Thursday. The mayor said the medal was undamaged, though he offered to pay for the cost of a new one. Goto, however, has accepted the International Olympic Committee's offer of a replacement, according to Japanese media reports. The scene broadcast on television prompted thousands of complaints to city hall. Some Olympians said they treat their medals as treasures and that it was disrespectful and unacceptable for Kawamura to bite one. "I would cry if that happened to me," said another athlete, Naohisa Takato."I handle my own gold medal so gently that I would not scratch it.”

M: What's that orange thing on your computer screen? W: It's something I bought yesterday. It's a plastic sheet that blocks blue light. I have one that I use to cover my phone screen too. M: What do you mean by blue light? W: Blue light includes natural light, but it also includes light that isn't natural, for example, from computers, phones, televisions and other electronic devices. M: So blue light is harmful and that's why you want to block it. W: It isn't that simple. Blue light isn't necessarily bad for us. In fact, we need blue light during the day to be healthy. But too much blue light, especially from electronic devices, can harm our health by weakening our vision and making it harder for us to fall asleep. And poor sleep can cause all sorts of health problems. M: I'm not so sure that sleep is nearly as important as people always say it is. I haven't slept enough in months because I have too much work to do, and I feel fine. And it's the same for most of my friends. Poor sleep might be a problem for older people, but surely young people can handle late nights. There is no indication of any digestive issues. M: So then why do I feel so poorly all the time? W: It's probably due to overwork and stress. M: No, it can't be. I've always been working hard, but I've never felt stress. Other people suffering complain about that, but I don't. It must be something else. W: What you have just described is a common sentiment. Many people who suffer from stress fail to recognise it. You told me you often work long into the night, right? M: Yes, most days in fact. But I've been doing that for about 20 years now. W: That doesn't matter. You could have been suffering from stress for 20 years without knowing it, and now it's catching up to you. M: But what about my feeling tired all the time and not being able to sleep well at night? W: Those are common consequences of stress. And if you don't sleep well, then of course you will feel fatigued. I'm going to prescribe some special sleeping pills for you. They have a soft, gentle effect and are made from natural ingredients, so your stomach should tolerate them fine, and there shouldn't be any negative side effects. Take one with your dinner and come see me after a month. If there is no improvement, I'll give you something stronger. M: Thank you, doctor. W: That's not all. You should try and work less. Is there any way you can decrease your workload? M: Um, I'd have to think about it. I'm a restaurant manager and this industry is very competitive. There are many things to keep track of and stay on top of. W: I recommend you think about delegating some responsibilities to someone else. I'm not asking you to retire. Just to slow down a bit. It's for your own health.

W: Today on People in the News, our guest is John Williams. The name may not sound familiar to you, but John was once an acclaimed basketball player. John, you stunned fans by leaving the sport at just 25. Why did you retire so early? M: Meg, I loved being an athlete, but I didn't love being a celebrity. I was in the limelight when I was still a high school student and went professional right after high school graduation, which was a mistake. I was a shy kid and I wasn't ready for all the media attention. W: But walking away from millions of dollars at the height of your career, most people wouldn't be able to resist the lure of such a high salary. When you left the sport, there was speculation that you were having issues with your teammates or even an injury. M: Not at all. It was hard to quit. I was tempted to stay in the game, because I love basketball and I loved my team. As for money, I turned professional at 18. So I'd actually earned a lot and saved most of it, because I had great financial advisers. I knew basketball wasn't a career with a lot of longevity for most players, so I wanted to change careers while I was still young. W: Okay, that was 20 years ago, and you're back in the news. You've created a foundation that works to get more kids playing team sports. Why? M: I went to university and I studied public health and learned about the seriousness of the obesity epidemic, particularly among kids and adolescents in poor communities. I've spent the last two decades trying to alleviate the problem. The foundation is just the latest attempt. W: The foundation uses private donations to support basketball teams for girls and boys in primary school, right? M: Actually, we support teams for secondary school students, too, and also have some public funding.

Kate Atkinson was born in York, England, in 1951. She worked hard to gain her credentials as an author. She studied English Literature at University in Scotland. After graduating in 1974, she researched a doctorate on American Literature. Later, she taught at the university she graduated from, and began writing short stories in 1981. She began writing for women's magazines after winning the 1986 Woman's Own Short Story Competition. Her first novel, Behind the Scenes at the Museum, won the 1995 UK Book of the Year award. The book is set in Yorkshire and has been adapted for radio, theatre, and TV. She has written two plays for a theatre in Edinburgh——the first was called Nice and the second Abandonment, performed as part of the Edinburgh Festival in August 2000. Whatever genre Atkinson writes in, her books touch on the themes of love and loss and how to carry on. They are always presented with ingenuity and a wicked sense of humor. Her books tend to be populated by odd, sometimes sinful, and generally flawed eccentrics who become credible by virtue of being so fully realized. Her books have frequently been described as comedies of manners. That is to say, comedies that represent the complex and sophisticated code of behaviour current in fashionable circles of society, where appearances count more than true moral character. A comedy of manners tends to reward its clever and deceitful characters, rather than punish their bad deeds. The humor of a comedy of manners relies on verbal wit and playful teasing.

Why is adaptability an important skill to exercise in the workplace? Simply put, adaptability is a skill employers are increasingly looking for. When you spend time learning a new task rather than resisting it, your productivity goes up. You can also serve as an example to your co-workers who may be having trouble adapting, and can help lead your team forward. Strategy consultant, Dorie Clark, explains it to us this way. 'I'd say that adaptability is an important skill in the workplace because frankly, circumstances change. Competitors introduce new products, economy might enter a recession, customer preferences differ over time, and more. If you shake your fist at the sky and say why can't it stay the same, that's not going to do very much good. Instead, you need to recognise when circumstances have changed, so you can take appropriate action based on what is, rather than how you wish the world would be. That enables you to make more accurate, informed and effective choices.” Also, the workplace itself has been evolving. Today's work culture and management style is often based on teamwork, rather than a rigid hierarchy. Brainstorming, which requires creativity, flexibility, and emotional intelligence, is a typical problem-solving technique. Employees who are unable or unwilling to participate will not easily move forward in the company. Employees who are flexible demonstrate other skills too. They can reprioritize quickly when changes occur and suggest additional modifications when something is not working. They can also regroup quickly when a setback occurs, adapting to the new situation confidently and without overreacting.

What makes humans different from other species? Some philosophers argue it's morals or ethics, while some scientists assert it's our greater cognitive development. But I argue that the main difference is our desire to combat routine. This makes being creative a biological mandate, as what we seek in art and technology is surprise, not simply a fulfillment of expectations. As a result, a wild imagination has characterized the history of our species. We build intricate habitats, devise complex recipes for our food, wear clothes that reflect constant changes in fashion, communicate with elaborate signs, symbols, and sounds, and travel between habitats on wings and wheels of our own design. To satisfy our appetite for novelty, innovation is key. But who innovates? Now, many people, both laymen and experts, believe that only geniuses innovate. But I believe that innovation is not something that only a few people do. The innovative drive lives in every human brain, and the resulting war against the repetitive is what powers the massive changes that distinguish one generation from the next. The drive to create the new is a trait of being human. We build cultures by the hundreds and tell new stories by the millions. We create and surround ourselves with things that have never existed before, while animals do not. But where do our new ideas come from? According to many, new ideas come from seemingly nowhere to great minds. From this perspective, new ideas are almost like magic. They come in a flash of inspiration to a select few. However, the reality is that, across the spectrum of human activities, prior work propels the creative process. We may think of innovation as being the result of inspiration or genius, but it's really the result of developing the ideas of others further. This happens in technology, where one invention enables or inspires further inventions. And it happens in the arts, as writers, composers, and painters use the work of previous artists in their own work. The human brain works from precedent. We take the ideas we've inherited and put them together into some new shape. What is a true creator? Is a creator a genius who makes something out of nothing? No. Creators are simply humans who use what they inherit, who absorb the past and manipulate it to create possible futures. Thus, humans are creators as a rule rather than as an exception.

Many dog owners would tell you that their dog somehow knows when they're ill or upset, and according to researchers who study dog cognition, those pet owners are right. Dogs do know when their human companions are having a rough time. Not only can your dog sense when you have a cold, but domestic dogs have shown an aptitude for detecting both much smaller mood fluctuations and far more serious physical conditions. This is because dogs are extremely sensitive to changes in the people they're familiar with, and illness causes change. If a person is infected with a virus or bacteria, for example, their odor will be abnormal, and dogs are able to smell that change even if the human can't, because dogs have a much more powerful sense of smell than humans. Researchers have also found that a person's mood, which can be an indicator of a larger illness, triggers a dog's sense of smell. Human emotions manifest physically in chemical signals that are emitted by the body, and dogs are able to smell those as well. Beyond smell, dogs gather information from a person's voice in order to sense changes. In 2014, researchers discovered that dogs have an area of the brain similar to one in humans that allows them to understand emotional cues in the tone of a speaker's voice, beyond what they'd be able to pick up from familiar words alone. A person's voice can also carry indicators of illness. What's not understood quite so well is what dogs understand about these changes. Humans send out lots of cues, but whether dogs know some of these cues mean illness isn't clear. What we perceive as concern on a dog's part might be more like increased curiosity or suspicion that something is wrong with us, and sticking close by is a great way to gather more information about the situation. Some researchers assert dogs will one day help doctors diagnose diseases, as some dogs have already demonstrated the ability to detect an assortment of ailments, including diabetes and certain types of cancer. But those researchers concede that's probably in the distant future. For now, research suggests dog ownership can have an array of benefits in and of itself. Keeping a pet dog has been shown to bolster health and boost mood. Dogs also help people relax, and they can be a particular comfort to those with chronic diseases.

Earlier this month, the think-tank called Onward published a report, "A Question of Degree”, which argues that degrees in the creative arts are not good value for money. Ministers, according to Onward, should “crack down on courses that offer extremely limited value for money to students ten years after graduation”, restricting the ability of such courses to recruit new students, if the average graduate earns below the student loans payment threshold. Courses like science, technology, engineering, and math, and economics, where the average graduate earns a lot, should be favored. The report provides insight into a government review which looks at how to reform technical education and how to ensure students get good value for money. At first glance, it might even seem like Onward have a point. According to their data, the majority of creative arts students earn less than 25,000 pounds a year, ten years after graduation. The average male creative arts students, indeed, apparently earn much less than they would, had they simply never gone to university. This isn't really good for anyone, and it's certainly no good for graduates, who are forced to endure a lifestyle where they can never save up, never buy a house, never hope to retire. Onward have identified a real problem. Creative arts graduates from top universities——like Oxford, with a high proportion of privately-educated students, have fairly good work prospects. Well, 40 percent of all graduates—regardless of their degree—are on less than 25,000 pounds a year, 5 years after graduation. This suggests that the problem isn't really to do with specific students studying specific degrees, but really with the economy as a whole. Regardless of what they've studied, young people find it hard to get ahead unless they're lucky enough to be born with successful parents. If ministers want to make education pay for young people, they need to look beyond the higher education sector, towards the wider world. The rewards that education gives us are not measurable. They are not always instantly obvious, and certainly not always direct. An education makes you a different person from the one you would have been if you hadn't received it. We need to look at the value of education not in the context of a bank balance, but of a life. If we continue to allow ourselves to be distracted with talk of “value for money”, we will all be made poorer as a result.

As is known to all, gaining a sound knowledge of the basics is of vital importance for students to master an academic subject.

Basic knowledge gives students a framework for understanding more complicated ideas. Without it, they may remember isolated facts but struggle to see how those facts fit together. A solid foundation also makes independent learning easier, because students can judge new information and connect it with what they already know.

My experience of learning mathematics illustrates this point. At first, I tried to solve difficult problems by copying methods from examples. This worked only when a new question looked familiar. After reviewing essential definitions and simple proofs, I could explain why each step was valid and adapt the method to unfamiliar questions. Progress became slower at the beginning but much more reliable later.

Students should therefore check their understanding of basic concepts, practise them regularly, and ask for feedback when an explanation remains unclear. Teachers can help by showing how advanced topics depend on earlier knowledge. Time spent building a foundation is an investment that enables deeper understanding and lasting progress.

30.hint: 先看第30空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。
30.explanation: O，upper。an upper limit表示上限，与下文no limit形成对照。将词填回本句可读为：“Contrary to some research that has found an upper limit to the amount of exercise that is healthy, the researchers found that there was [31] ____ no limit to the longevity (长寿) benefits of exercise.”。其他选项即使词性相同，也需同时符合这句话所表达的含义。

31.hint: 先看第31空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。
31.explanation: M，seemingly。副词修饰没有上限的判断，意为看起来似乎。将词填回本句可读为：“Contrary to some research that has found an [30] ____ limit to the amount of exercise that is healthy, the researchers found that there was seemingly no limit to the longevity (长寿) benefits of exercise.”。其他选项即使词性相同，也需同时符合这句话所表达的含义。

32.hint: 先看第32空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。

38.explanation: 对应B段。BBC Future说明近期新闻，植物基因与无水存活说明基因工程帮助抗旱，两个信息结合。 该段证据（合看相关句）：“It’s clear that farmers in many parts of the world are going to find things harder in the coming decades. Last week, BBC Future explored one scientist’s efforts to help crops cope with the increased probability of droughts. 39.explanation: 对应G段。less available说明供应减少，pay a lot more说明涨价；可可产量变化是原因，末句给出结果。 该段证据（合看相关句）：“Under current conditions, about 4% of the world’s croplands experience drought in any given year, but by the end of the century those conditions are forecasted to jump to about 18% per year. Some studies indicate that horticulture crops — generally, everything besides staples — may be impacted most severely, largely because they tend to be confined to a smaller geographic area. Researcher Andrew Jarvis and his colleagues found that 80% of coffee-growing zones in Central America and Brazil could become unsuitable by 2050, for example, while climate change will likely have “great impacts” on cocoa (可可粉) production in West Africa. “High quality chocolate will be less available in the future, and if you want it, you’ll have to pay a lot more for it,” Jarvis says.”

41.explanation: 对应F段。向北移动只能到一定程度，后文说土壤质量使产量仍可能受损，两个条件须合看。 该段证据（合看相关句）：“In the U.S. — the world’s largest producer of corn and soybeans — farms can move north to some degree, Schlenker says. But eventually, yields will likely suffer because the soil north of Iowa declines in quality — a legacy of glacial (冰川的) expansion. Other studies, including studies of wheat in India and corn in Africa, also found that there is a threshold above which yields sharply decline: crops can adapt and move, but only to a point. “What’s common to all studies is the finding that extreme heat is damaging to crop growth, although exact cutoffs vary by crop,” Schlenker says. “If predictions for the end of the century are true, though, I think a lot of agricultural areas in the U.S. will see significant hits.””

42.explanation: 对应L段。题干陈述为“One possible solution to the food security problem is diversification of diet.”；该段的关键证据是：“Finally, diversifying our diet away from heat-sensitive wheat, corn, rice and other crops could also help.”。同时对照主体、行为和结果，不能只凭同一个词匹配；这份陈述概括了该段的对应信息。

43.hint: 先圈出陈述里的主体、条件和变化方向，再到文章中寻找同义表达。
43.explanation: 对应J段。the jury is still out表示尚无定论；those endeavours指耐旱耐热作物的基因工程育种努力。 该段证据（合看相关句）：“There are ways we could soften the coming blow to the global food supply, however. Like Farrant’s work with resurrection crops, a number of companies, organisations and researchers are aiming to create drought- and temperature-resistant crops through genetic engineering and conventional breeding. For now, the jury is still out as to how successful those endeavours will be. “The people at Monsanto who I’ve talked to are much more optimistic that they’ll be able to engineer heat-tolerant crops,” Schlenker says. “On the other hand, scientists at the USDA who I’ve spoken with are much more cautious.””

26.hint: 先看第26空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。

28.hint: 先看第28空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。
28.explanation: I，normal。than normal表示比平时花更长时间。将词填回本句可读为：“The researchers found that when participants spent longer than normal on their leisure activity, their belief in their ability to perform their job was strengthened.”。其他选项即使词性相同，也需同时符合这句话所表达的含义。

29.hint: 先看第29空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。
29.explanation: B，case。only the case表示只在特定条件下才成立。将词填回本句可读为：“But this was only the case when they had a serious hobby that was dissimilar to their job, or when their hobby was similar to their work but they only did it [30] ____.”。其他选项即使词性相同，也需同时符合这句话所表达的含义。

30.hint: 先看第30空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。
30.explanation: C，casually。副词修饰did，表示随意而非认真从事爱好。将词填回本句可读为：“But this was only the [29] ____ when they had a serious hobby that was dissimilar to their job, or when their hobby was similar to their work but they only did it casually.”。其他选项即使词性相同，也需同时符合这句话所表达的含义。

31.hint: 先看第31空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。
31.explanation: D，efficiency。work efficiency为工作效率，花更多时间可能使其下降。将词填回本句可读为：“When their hobby was both serious and similar to their job, then spending more time on it actually decreased their work efficiency.”。其他选项即使词性相同，也需同时符合这句话所表达的含义。

32.hint: 先看第32空的句法位置和前后搭配，再结合整段话的语义判断。
32.explanation: F，exhausted。left后形容词补足语，说明心理资源耗尽而疲惫。将词填回本句可读为：“To maintain a serious hobby, people need to invest significant psychological resources, say the authors—so if the activity has the same kinds of demands as their work, they may be left exhausted and unable to perform well at their job.”。其他选项即使词性相同，也需同时符合这句话所表达的含义。
